newsitem.title: POLAND: POLES QUEUE TO BE CAPITALISTS IN SELL-OFF SCHEME.
newsitem.headline: POLES QUEUE TO BE CAPITALISTS IN SELL-OFF SCHEME.

text.p: Long forgotten communist-era style queues returned to Polish cities as hundreds of thousands of eligible adults rushed to beat the Friday deadline for picking up units in the country's mass privatisation programme.
Poles have been flocking for the last two weeks at PKO BP bank's 1,200 outlets to buy certificates in the scheme before the end of the 12-month distribution period.
The certificates are to be exchanged next year for shares in 15 National Investment Funds (NFIs) created to manage and privatise more than 500 small and medium-sized companies.

The unit, which each citizen can initially buy for 20 zlotys ($7.1), now trades at around 150 zlotys ($53.6) at the bourse and exchange offices, so many Poles are content to take a quick profit while others ponder becoming shareholders for the first time in their lives.

"I don't know much of what this is all about but why waste 100 zlotys...even if this means seven hours in a queue," said retired construction worker Bogdan Michalak, who has a pension of some 500 zlotys ($178.5) a month.
He arrived at a Warsaw banking outlet at 5.00 a.m. to discover about 40 people before him. By 9.00 a.m. when the bank opened there were well above 100 waiting in line.

"Poles are simply like that. They always wait for the last moment with everything. I live just next to the bank and had thousands of opportunites to buy my unit," said Irena Dziwisz, in her early twenties.
At many banks "queue committees" were formed, reviving long-obsolete communist-era techniques to allow people take turns in long lines.

"We haven't seen anything like this since the times of the (communist) People's Republic of Poland, when people queued like this for a washing machine or a TV set," said PKO BP spokesman Janusz Ostaszewski.
Ostaszewski estimated that more than 25 million people will have bought the unit by the end of the sale on Friday evening -- about 90 percent of those eligible.

"This is a great success. It shows confidence in the programme," said Wieslaw Kaczmarek, deputy treasury minister and the former privatisation portfolio head, who supervised the launch of the programme.
More than 300,000 units a day were being sold in the final week, official figures showed.

A recent survey by the private Demoskop agency showed that nearly 50 percent Poles who had bought the unit have already sold it on the secondary market and seven percent more planned to do so in near future. These were mainly the young, the low-paid and the uneducated, Demoskop said.
The poll indicated that about 23 percent of those who bought the unit planned to keep it or even buy more.
Kaczmarek said it would take about two years before the economic effects of the scheme could be properly assessed.

Earlier this week Kaczmarek said the popular enthusiasm was a blow to critics of the scheme. These include the Solidarity union, which argues that Poland should have distributed shares to the public in all state-owned assets, not just 500 firms. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
